Full Explanation:

Consider the equation \(x^{m}=y^{2}+1\) with \(x,m,y \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}\).

Case 1: \(m=1\).
We have \(x=y^{2}+1\). Every positive integer \(y\) gives a solution, so the set \(\{(x,m,y)=(y^{2}+1,1,y): y\in\mathbb{N}\}\) is a solution.

Next we show there is no solution when \(m\ge2\).

Firstly, if \(m\) is even, say \(m=2k\) (\(k\ge1\)). Then
\[
x^{2k}=y^{2}+1\Longrightarrow (x^{k})^{2}-y^{2}=1
\Longrightarrow (x^{k}-y)(x^{k}+y)=1.
\]
Both factors are positive integers; the only factorisation of 1 is \(1\cdot1\). This gives
\(x^{k}=1\) and \(y=0\), contradicting \(y>0\). Thus \(m\) cannot be even.

Hence any possible exponent \(m>1\) must be odd, write \(m=2k+1\ (k\ge1)\).

Now work in the ring of Gaussian integers \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\). We have
\[
x^{m}=y^{2}+1=(y+i)(y-i).
\]
Let \(d=\gcd(y+i,y-i)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\). Since \(d\mid (y+i)-(y-i)=2i\) and \(2=(-i)(1+i)^{2}\) is a square in \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\), the only possible common divisor is a unit; we may therefore assume \(\gcd(y+i,y-i)=1\). (If the common divisor is \((1+i)\) we divide both factors by \((1+i)\); this changes the equation to a still‑valid one with the same exponent because \((1+i)^{2}=-2\) is a perfect square.)

Since the two coprime factors multiply to an \(m\)‑th power, each factor itself must be an \(m\)‑th power up to a unit. Thus there exists a Gaussian integer \(a+bi\) and a unit \(\varepsilon\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}\) such that
\[
y+i=\varepsilon (a+bi)^{m},\qquad
y-i=\bar{\varepsilon}\,(a-bi)^{m}.
\]
Taking imaginary parts we obtain
\[
\operatorname{Im}\big((a+bi)^{m}\big)=\pm1.
\]

Write \((a+bi)^{m}=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\binom{m}{j}a^{\,m-j}(bi)^{j}\).
The imaginary part is
\[
\operatorname{Im}\big((a+bi)^{m}\big)=\sum_{\substack{j\text{ odd}}}\binom{m}{j}a^{\,m-j}b^{j}(-1)^{(j-1)/2}.
\]
Every term in this sum is an integer multiple of \(b\). In particular the whole sum is divisible by \(b\). Since its absolute value is 1, we must have \(|b|=1\).

Put \(b=\pm1\). Then the imaginary part becomes
\[
\pm\Bigl(\binom{m}{1}a^{\,m-1} \mp \binom{m}{3}a^{\,m-3} + \dots\Bigr)=\pm1.
\]
Reducing modulo \(a\) we see that \(\binom{m}{1}a^{\,m-1}\equiv\pm1\pmod a\); but \(\binom{m}{1}=m\) and for any integer \(a\ge1\) the left‑hand side is a multiple of \(a\) unless \(a=1\). Consequently \(a=1\).

Thus \((a,b)=(1,\pm1)\). The norm of \(a+bi\) is \(|a+bi|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=2\). Hence
\[
x^{m}=|(y+i)|^{2}=|(a+bi)^{m}|^{2}=|a+bi|^{2m}=2^{m}.
\]
Therefore \(x=2\) and \(2^{m}=x^{m}=2^{m}\) holds for all \(m\). But then the original equation would read
\[
2^{m}=y^{2}+1.
\]
The only power of two that is one more than a square is \(2^{3}=8\) (since \(8+1=9=3^{2}\)). However \(8\) is not a perfect square, and in our case we need \(y^{2}=2^{m}-1\). Checking the few possibilities yields:
\[
2^{1}-1=1=1^{2},\quad 2^{2}-1=3\text{ non‑square},\quad 2^{3}-1=7\text{ non‑square},\dots
\]
Indeed, the equation \(y^{2}=2^{m}-1\) has only the solution \(m=1, y=1\); this forces \(m=1\), contradicting the assumption \(m>1\).

Hence our hypothesis \(m>1\) leads to a contradiction. Therefore there are no solutions with \(m\ge2\).

Summarizing, the complete set of positive integer solutions of \(x^{m}=y^{2}+1\) is

\[
\boxed{ \{ (x,m,y)=(y^{2}+1,\ 1,\ y) \mid y\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} \} }.
\]

(If one accepts Mihăilescu’s theorem (Catalan’s conjecture) the same result follows immediately: for \(m>1\) we would have a non‑trivial solution to \(x^{m}-y^{2}=1\), which Catalan’s theorem forbids.)

Thus the only positive integer solutions occur when \(m=1\), i.e., \(x=y^{2}+1\).<|end_think|>\[
x^{m}=y^{2}+1 ,\qquad x,m,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0}
\]

---

### 1.  The case  \(m=1\)

If \(m=1\) the equation becomes  

\[
x=y^{2}+1 .
\]

For every positive integer \(y\) we obtain a solution  

\[
(x,m,y)=(y^{2}+1,\;1,\;y).
\]

Thus an infinite family of solutions exists when \(m=1\).

---

### 2.  No solutions for \(m\ge 2\)

Assume now that \(m\ge2\).

#### 2.1  \(m\) cannot be even  

Write \(m=2k\;(k\ge1)\). Then  

\[
x^{2k}=y^{2}+1\Longrightarrow (x^{k})^{2}-y^{2}=1
      \Longrightarrow (x^{k}-y)(x^{k}+y)=1 .
\]

Both factors are positive integers; the only factorisation of 1 is \(1\cdot1\).  
Hence \(x^{k}=1\) and \(y=0\), contradicting \(y>0\).  
Therefore **\(m\) must be odd**.

#### 2.2  Work in the Gaussian integers  

Write the equation as  

\[
x^{m}=y^{2}+1=(y+i)(y-i) .
\]

In \(\mathbb Z[i]\) any common divisor of the two factors divides their difference  
\((y+i)-(y-i)=2i\).  Since \(2=(-i)(1+i)^{2}\) is a perfect square in \(\mathbb Z[i]\),
the two factors are coprime up to a unit.  Consequently each factor must be an
\(m\)‑th power (up to a unit).  Hence there exist a Gaussian integer
\(a+bi\) and a unit \(\varepsilon\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}\) such that  

\[
y+i=\varepsilon (a+bi)^{m}, \qquad   
y-i=\bar\varepsilon\,(a-bi)^{m}.
\]

Taking imaginary parts gives  

\[
\operatorname{Im}\big((a+bi)^{m}\big)=\pm1. \tag{1}
\]

---

#### 2.3  The imaginary part forces \(|b|=1\)

Expanding \((a+bi)^{m}\),

\[
\operatorname{Im}\big((a+bi)^{m}\big)=
\sum_{\substack{j\ \text{odd}}}
\binom{m}{j}a^{\,m-j}b^{j}(-1)^{\frac{j-1}{2}} .
\]

Every term on the right is a multiple of \(b\); therefore the whole sum is
divisible by \(b\).  Because of (1) its absolute value is \(1\), so \(|b|=1\).

Put \(b=\pm1\).  Then (1) becomes  

\[
\pm\Bigl(\binom{m}{1}a^{\,m-1}\mp\binom{m}{3}a^{\,m-3}
        \pm\cdots\Bigr)=\pm1 .
\]

The left‑hand side is divisible by \(a\) unless \(a=1\).  Hence \(a=1\).

Thus \((a,b)=(1,\pm1)\).  Its norm is  

\[
|a+bi|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=2 .
\]

---

#### 2.4  Consequences for \(x\)

From \(y+i=\varepsilon (a+bi)^{m}\) we obtain  

\[
x^{m}=|(y+i)|^{2}=|(a+bi)^{m}|^{2}
        =|a+bi|^{2m}=2^{\,m}.
\]

Hence \(x=2\) and the original equation reduces to  

\[
2^{\,m}=y^{2}+1 .
\]

The only power of two that is one more than a square is \(2^{1}=2\) (since
\(2-1=1=1^{2}\)); for \(m\ge2\) the numbers \(2^{\,m}-1\) are never perfect
squares.  Thus \(m=1\), contradicting the assumption \(m\ge2\).

Therefore **no solution exists when \(m\ge2\).**

---

### 3.  Solution set

The only positive–integer solutions of

\[
x^{m}=y^{2}+1
\]

are those with exponent \(m=1\).  Consequently

\[
\boxed{\;(x,m,y)=(y^{2}+1,\;1,\;y),\qquad y\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\; } .
\]

In other words, for every positive integer \(y\) the triple
\((y^{2}+1,\,1,\,y)\) solves the equation, and there are no solutions with
\(m>1\).  (The impossibility for \(m>1\) may also be deduced directly from
Mihăilescu’s theorem – Catalan’s conjecture – which states that the only
consecutive perfect powers are \(8\) and \(9\).)<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
